might produce environmental regulations more favorable, depending on 
the case, to industry or to conservationists. Yet, courts are reluctant to find 
that an executive order “confers” a private right of action to secure an 
agency’s compliance with the order’s obhgations. See, e.g., Manhcittan- 
Bronx Postal Union v. Gronouski, 350 F.2d 451 (D.C. Cir. 1965), cert, 
denied, 382 U.S. 978 (1966); Stevens v. Carey, 483 F.2d 188 (7th Cir. 1973). 
The rationale behind this reluctance varies. In some cases, a court may 
resist enforcing an order because, as is the case in many modern orders, 
the text explicitly disavows private enforceability. See, e.g., Louisiana ex 
rel. Guste v. Verity, 853 F.2d 322 (5th Cir. 1988) (holding Executive Order 
No. 12,291 requirement for regulatory analysis not judicially enforceable). 
Probably the most comprehensive and detailed presidential disavowal of 
enforceability appears in Executive Order 12,778, § 6, 56 Fed. Reg. 55,195, 
55,200 (1991), requiring federal litigators to act in a variety of ways to 
reduce the “burdens and costs” imposed by civil litigation in which the 
gnvAmmerit is involved. In other cases, courts have determined that— 
irrespective of presidential intent—^the president lacks inherent power to 
create judicially enforceable government obligations without congressional 
authorization. See In re Surface Mining Pegulation Litigation, ^2,1 F.2d 
1346 (D.C. Cir. 1980) (holding Executive Order No. 11,821, requiring 
inflation impact analysis, not judicially enforceable).
Especially—^though not exclusively—in periods of divided government, 
executive orders can be important instruments for conducting the 
president’s ongoing policy dialogues with Congress. They can be used to 
maintain the status quo in a particular context pursuant to a shared 
expectation that Congress will subsequently act on the same subject. A 
prominent, example is President Carter’s December 1, 1978, issuance of 
fifteen proclamations designating about a third of Alaska as national 
monuments, in order to prevent their private development prior to 
Congress’s completion of its work on what became the 1980 Alaska 
National Interest Lands Conservation Act, Pub. L. No. 96—487, 94 Stat. 
2371 (1980). Cf. President Taft’s Temporary Petroleum Withdrawal No. 5, 
upheld in United States v. Midwest Oil Co., supra, preventing the private 
development of U.S. oil lands in anticipation of military needs.
Executive orders can also be used to demonstrate initiative in areas on 
which the President seeks legislation, but Congress either actively resists 
or is simply unable to achieve consensus. Prominent subjects for such 
orders during the Obama presidency included gun control (see, e.g.. 
Memorandum for the Heads of Exec. Dep’ts and Agencies re: Tracing of 
Firearms in Connection with Criminal Investigations, 78 Fed. Reg. 4301
